CausalChain: Chronic biliary inflammation -> Activation of CAFs -> Secretion of exosomes enriched in microRNAs -> Uptake by cholangiocytes -> Induction of epigenetic modifications (hypermethylation, e.g., suppression of tumor suppressors like ARID1A) -> Presence of IDH1/2 mutations leading to 2-hydroxyglutarate accumulation -> Further enhancement of DNA hypermethylation -> Promotion of EMT and CSC traits -> Increased chemoresistance and tumor progression
Hypothesis: In cholangiocarcinoma, a synergistic interaction between CAF-derived exosomal microRNAs and IDH1/2 mutation-mediated epigenetic reprogramming drives EMT and cancer stem cell phenotype, which in turn fosters chemoresistance and tumor aggressiveness. Targeting this feed-forward loop may offer novel therapeutic opportunities.
Abstract: This hypothesis explores a novel interplay between the tumor microenvironment and intrinsic genetic alterations in the progression and treatment resistance of cholangiocarcinoma. We propose that cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) within the desmoplastic stroma secrete exosomes enriched with regulatory microRNAs that, when taken up by cholangiocytes, induce epigenetic modifications. In cholangiocarcinomas harboring IDH1/2 mutations, the accumulation of the oncometabolite 2-hydroxyglutarate further promotes a hypermethylated state, collectively facilitating the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and acquisition of cancer stem cell (CSC) characteristics. This synergistic mechanism is suggesting a feed-forward loop that enhances chemoresistance and tumor aggressiveness, thereby providing a potential target for therapeutic intervention.
